challenge.proof: Send me (Claude) the link to your positioning post, a screenshot or PDF of Radar #1, the two pitch emails as sent, and your one-page Summit plan. Save them all in a folder called 'Proof - Claim Your Crown'.
challenge.bonus: Get a reply from one partner and book a 20-minute call, or record a 60-second video of your bilingual introduction and post it.

quiz.question: Which line best shows a 'category of one'?
options: I do websites, logos, posts and translation for everyone
The supplier-readiness studio for Mozambique's gas and mining supply chain
The cheapest web designer in Maputo
quiz.explanation: It is narrow, clear about who it serves and why it matters, and hard to compare with a general web designer.

quiz.question: You want to write a post with the exact Law 9/2026 thresholds. What should you do first?
options: Copy the numbers from the first news article you find
Read the official Boletim da República text and verify the numbers
Use the numbers from the earlier bill, since they are similar
quiz.explanation: Sources disagree on the thresholds, so only the official text is safe to quote. Also say it is a plain-language summary, not legal advice.

quiz.question: A consultancy sends you a client. How do you handle the referral fee?
options: Pay it secretly so the client does not ask for a discount
Refuse all referral fees
Pay it and make sure the client knows about it
Pay the client's procurement contact instead
quiz.explanation: A disclosed referral fee is honest business. Hidden payments, or payments to people inside the buyer, cross the ethics wall.

glossary.meaning: The clear place your business holds in a client's mind.
Describing your work so narrowly that you have no direct comparison.
A public call where a big buyer asks suppliers to show they are interested and qualified.
A payment to a partner who sends you a paying client, always disclosed to the client.
The moment the owners formally commit the money to build a big project.
A programme that supports young businesses with training, mentors and contacts.

chapters.title: Run Yourself Like a Company
chapters.subtitle: Metrics, rhythm, money and the 12-month road
chapters.mentor_intro:
Here is a truth nobody tells you when you start alone: you are now the boss, the employee, the accountant and the cleaner. Nobody will check if you sent your 20 outreaches today. Nobody will tell you to stop working at 23:00. Freedom feels wonderful on Monday. By Wednesday, when nobody replies, it can feel very heavy.

That is why this last chapter is about you. Not about clients, not about documents. About how you run yourself. A company has a weekly meeting, clear numbers, a budget, a plan and rules. You will have the same, even if the company is only one person with a laptop.

I will show you the weekly CEO hour, a daily rhythm that protects your energy, how to treat rejection as data, how to manage money so it does not disappear, and a 12-month roadmap. At the end there is a final boss: a 30-day sprint. I believe you can finish it. Not because it is easy, but because you will follow a system.
learning_goals: Run a weekly CEO hour and read your own business numbers
Organise your day in time blocks that protect your energy and health
Respond to rejection and slow weeks by changing one variable at a time
Manage business money: separate accounts, a money log, fixed pay, an emergency fund and a tax set-aside
Follow a 12-month roadmap, and say no to bad clients and bad deals

sections.heading: The weekly CEO hour

blocks.text: Every Friday, for one hour, you stop working **in** the business and work **on** the business. This is your **CEO hour (hora do director)**. You look at your numbers, decide what to change, and plan next week. Keep everything in one simple spreadsheet called your **scoreboard (quadro de resultados)**.

blocks.title: The seven numbers on your scoreboard
The CEO hour agenda
items: Spend 10 minutes updating the scoreboard with this week's numbers.
Spend 10 minutes on simple ratios, for example replies divided by outreaches.
Spend 15 minutes writing what worked and what did not, three lines each.
Spend 15 minutes choosing ONE thing to change next week.
Spend 10 minutes preparing Monday's list of companies, so Monday starts fast.

blocks.title: Practice numbers (invented, only to practise the maths)
blocks.text:
Imagine a week with 100 outreaches, 6 replies, 2 calls, 1 proposal for Supplier-Ready and 0 deposits. Your reply ratio is 6 out of 100. Your **pipeline value (valor em negociação)** is 65,000 MT, because one proposal is still open.

The lesson is not 'I failed'. The lesson is: 'The weak point is between replies and calls. Next week I will improve how I ask for the call.' These numbers are only an exercise. Your real numbers will be different.

sections.heading: Daily rhythm, energy and health

blocks.title: A sample weekday (adjust it to your life)
rows: A real meal, away from the screen

blocks.text: Outreach goes first in the morning because it is the task you will most want to avoid. Do the hard thing while your energy is high. Delivery comes right after. Chapter 1 showed delivery first; both orders work. When a client deadline is close, swap the two blocks, because paying clients come before everything else.

blocks.title: Protect your energy
items: Sleep at the same time most nights. A tired brain writes bad emails.
Eat real meals. Do not live on bread and soft drinks while you work.
Take a short break every 90 minutes: stand up, walk, drink water.
Put your phone on silent during outreach and delivery blocks.
Take one full day off every week. Rest is part of the job.

blocks.text: Here is a pattern I want you to avoid. Someone works 14 hours a day for two weeks, gets no deposit, feels empty, and quits. Someone else works 7 focused hours a day for two months, and builds something. Your business must survive a bad week. Build a rhythm you can keep.

sections.heading: Rejection, slow weeks and the learning plan

blocks.text: Rejection is not a verdict on you. It is data about your message.

Most people you contact will not reply. Some will say no. A 'no' is final: thank them and do not contact them again. But a slow week is information. Your job is to read it calmly, like an engineer reads a broken machine.

blocks.title: What to do in a slow week
items: Check the basics: did you really send 20 outreaches every weekday and do the Day 3 and Day 7 follow-ups?
If not, the problem is volume. Fix that first, before you change anything else.
If yes, choose ONE variable to change: subject line, first sentence, city, sector, or the question that asks for the call.
Keep everything else the same for one full week.
Compare the numbers in your next CEO hour. Keep the change if it helped. Try the next variable if it did not.

blocks.text: Change one thing at a time. If you change the subject, the sector and the city in the same week, you will never know which change made the difference.

blocks.title: 30 minutes of learning a day
rows: Read one real EOI PDF fully
Study the layout of a good profile
Practise the H5 call script out loud

sections.heading: Money management

blocks.title: Six money rules
items: Separate business money: use one bank account or one mobile money wallet only for the business.
Keep a money log: date, client, amount, method, and the receipt number with your NUIT.
Pay yourself a fixed amount every month, the same amount, even in a good month.
Build an emergency fund (fundo de emergência) before you buy anything nice.
Set aside money for tax from every payment, and confirm the real amount with the tax authority (AT) or an accountant.
Reinvest in tools that pay back: a domain, data bundles, and later a better laptop.

blocks.title: Fictional example: one Supplier-Ready payment
blocks.text: Imagine 65,000 MT arrives for a project. It goes into the business account, not your pocket. From there you take: a tax set-aside (the amount your accountant confirms), your fixed monthly pay (an amount you choose and keep stable, for example 15,000 MT), a part for the emergency fund, and a small part for tools. What remains stays in the business for slow months. The exact split is your decision. The habit is what matters.

The simplified tax for small taxpayers (ISPC, Imposto Simplificado para Pequenos Contribuintes) was reportedly changed recently (Law 9/2025), but the rates and thresholds are not verified. Ask the AT or an accountant before you calculate anything. For large B2B payments, use bank transfer with a receipt that shows your NUIT. An individual M-Pesa account has a daily limit of 200,000 MT. Always confirm payments in your own app, never from a screenshot.

**When to raise prices:** after proof. A good moment is after 3 happy clients with written testimonials. The launch price for the first 3 clients was real scarcity, so ending it is honest. Raise prices for new clients only, keep your word to current clients, and announce it in advance. If someone cannot pay, offer a smaller package, a **downsell (oferta mais pequena)**, instead of a discount.

blocks.title: Announcing the end of the launch price
blocks.text: Bom dia, Sr. [Apelido]. Uma informação rápida: o preço de lançamento para os três primeiros clientes terminou. A partir de [data], o pacote Supplier-Ready passa a custar [novo preço] MT. As propostas já enviadas mantêm o preço até ao fim do prazo de validade indicado. Fico ao dispor para qualquer esclarecimento.

sections.heading: The 12-month roadmap

blocks.text: **SOPs (procedimentos operacionais padrão)** are written step-by-step instructions for work you repeat: onboarding, the 7-day plan, quality control, handover. Every time you deliver, improve the SOP a little. After five projects, delivery is faster and calmer, and someone else could follow it.

Bring in a freelance designer only when you have more work than time. Start with one small paid job and a short written agreement that includes confidentiality. Always check the quality yourself before the client sees it. The client trusts you, not the subcontractor.

Think about registering a company (**sociedade por quotas, Lda**) when your income is regular, not on day one. An accountant can explain the costs and obligations for your situation. Some big clients may prefer a registered supplier, but many companies first ask for a factura or recibo with your NUIT.

sections.heading: Saying no, and who you have become

blocks.title: Signs of a bad client or a bad deal
items: Asks you to inflate their HSE record, capabilities or ownership
Refuses the 50% deposit 'because we are a big company'
Wants a guarantee that they will win a contract
Suggests a payment to someone to 'get on the vendor list'
Offers to pay by a strange method, or asks you to pay a 'fee to receive'
Asks for free work again and again, or treats you with disrespect

blocks.title: A polite, firm no
blocks.text: Exmo. Sr. [Apelido], agradeço muito o vosso interesse e a confiança. Infelizmente, não posso incluir nos documentos informação que não esteja comprovada, porque isso pode prejudicar a vossa empresa nos processos de selecção de fornecedores. Se preferirem trabalhar apenas com factos documentados, terei todo o gosto em ajudar. Caso contrário, desejo-vos muito sucesso.

Look back at Chapter 1. You started with a laptop, two languages, no contacts and no portfolio. Now you know how a supply chain works, what an EOI asks for, how to start a conversation with a director, how to write a proposal, how to deliver in 7 days, and how to protect your name. Whatever your scoreboard says this month, you are not the same person who opened this book. You are someone who builds.
Clients pay for documents. They come back for the person who never cut a corner.

key_takeaways: Every Friday, hold a CEO hour: update the scoreboard, choose one change, plan Monday.
Do outreach first in the morning, protect your sleep, and take one day off a week.
Rejection is data: check volume first, then change one variable at a time.
Separate business money, pay yourself a fixed amount, and confirm tax with the AT or an accountant.
Raise prices only after proof, and build SOPs so delivery gets faster.
Saying no to bad clients protects your business and your name.

challenge.title: The 30-Day Sprint (Final Boss)
challenge.mission: For 30 days you run yourself like a real company. You do the daily outreach, the weekly CEO hour, the calls, the proposals and at least one delivery, and you track everything. At the end you send me your scoreboard, and we read it together.
steps: Create your scoreboard in a free Google Sheet with the seven metrics from this chapter, one row per day.

Send 20 value-first outreaches every weekday within the safety limits: about 30 cold emails per day maximum, WhatsApp permission first, no more than 15 new WhatsApp contacts per hour, and a 'no' is final.
Do every Day 3 and Day 7 follow-up on the same email thread.
Hold your CEO hour every Friday, and write down your one change for the next week.
Book and complete at least 5 calls using the H5 script.
Send at least 3 proposals, each within 30 minutes of the call.
Deliver 1 project or pilot using the 7-day plan from Chapter 10.
challenge.proof: Send me (Claude) your final scoreboard, your Friday CEO-hour notes, and one delivered file (with the client's permission, or your own pilot). Save everything in a folder called 'Proof - 30-Day Sprint'.
challenge.bonus: Close one Monthly Growth Retainer or collect one written testimonial with permission to publish, and write a one-page SOP for the part of your work you repeated most.

quiz.question: In a slow week you sent only 40 outreaches instead of 100. What should you change first?
options: The subject line
The target sector and city
The volume: get back to 20 outreaches every weekday
Your prices
quiz.explanation: If the volume is low, you cannot judge the message. Fix the basics first, then change one variable at a time.

quiz.question: A client pays 65,000 MT. What is the best first move?
options: Spend it on a new laptop to celebrate
Put it in the business account, log it, and split it by your money rules
Keep it in your personal wallet with your other money
quiz.explanation: Separate business money and a money log are the base of everything: fixed pay, tax set-aside, emergency fund and reinvestment.

quiz.question: When is a good moment to raise your prices?
options: After your very first enquiry
After proof, for example 3 happy clients with written testimonials
Never, because low prices win more clients
Whenever a client asks for a discount
quiz.explanation: Raise prices after proof, for new clients only, and announce it in advance. Offer a smaller package instead of a discount.

The total value of proposals that are still open and could still close.
